aspectTitle: Instruction promised on focus does not actually become perceivable when the field is focused
aspectDescription: WCAG explicitly blesses the pattern of withholding a long/verbose instruction until the field receives focus, and Trusted Tester makes 'visible when the form field has focus' a normative requirement. The conformance question is therefore behavioral: when the field is focused, does the promised instruction (password-complexity rule, date-format hint, character rules) actually become visible? The failure is a field whose only instruction is wired to appear on focus but in fact (a) never appears, (b) appears empty/placeholder-only, (c) appears off-screen / clipped / behind another element, (d) au
scenario: Fintech (Tellard) wallet signup. The password field's only instruction is its complexity rules ('12+ chars, 1 number, 1 symbol'), deferred to a display:none div meant to reveal on focus. The reveal handler removes the WRONG class name (classList.remove('hide') instead of 'hidden'), a silent no-op, so the rules stay display:none in every state. On focus the field shows only empty space — the only instruction never appears.
mechanism: The focus handler calls classList.remove('hide') on #pw-rules, but the hiding class is 'hidden'; remove() of an absent class is a no-op, so '.hidden{display:none}' is never lifted. The rules node stays display:none, is pruned from the AX tree, and the aria-describedby='pw-rules' association resolves to a hidden node — the field's only instruction is never perceivable on focus (or any state). Verified headless: hint stays display:none / rect 0x0 / not in viewport after driving keyboard focus.

scenario: Brightleaf Coffee Co. checkout payment step. The promo-code field accepts only format 'ABC-1234' (three letters, dash, four digits) — the field's only instruction. The hint is revealed by a CSS '.promo-wrap:hover .promo-hint' rule ONLY; there is no :focus / :focus-within rule. A mouse user who hovers sees the format; a keyboard user who tabs to the field gets nothing.
mechanism: Reveal is gated purely on :hover of the wrapper. On keyboard focus the hint stays opacity:0; max-height:0; overflow:hidden (collapsed, imperceptible). Verified headless: after page.focus(#promo) the hint reports opacity 0 / height 18 collapsed; only after page.hover(#promo) does it reach opacity 1 / height 50. Keyboard and most screen-reader users (who reach the field by focus, not hover) never receive the format instruction.

scenario: Aerolink flight-booking date step. The travel-date field requires day-first format 'DD/MM/YYYY' — its only instruction. The hint is a 'floating help bar' (position:fixed; bottom:0) revealed on focus, but a booking-summary footer is ALSO position:fixed; bottom:0 with a higher z-index and opaque background. Both pin to the viewport bottom, so on focus the revealed hint paints directly behind the opaque footer and is fully occluded in every viewport.
mechanism: #travel:focus ~ .date-hint sets display:block and the hint is visibility:visible/opacity:1 on focus, but .date-hint (position:fixed; bottom:0; z-index:10) and .summary-bar (position:fixed; bottom:0; z-index:50, opaque) share the bottom band, so the footer paints over the hint. Verified headless: after driving keyboard focus, document.elementFromPoint at the hint's center returns .summary-bar (not the hint) at viewports 800x600, 1024x768, 1280x900 and 1440x1024 — occlusion is deterministic across heights.

scenario: Thornwood Makers community-forum signup. The username rules ('3-20 chars; letters/numbers/hyphens/underscores; must start with a letter') are the field's only instruction. On focus the tooltip fades in correctly, but a setTimeout(...,1500) then fades it out and sets aria-hidden while the field still has focus — it auto-dismisses before a slow reader finishes and does not return unless the field is blurred and re-focused.
mechanism: The focus handler adds class 'show' then, 1500ms later, runs tip.classList.remove('show'); tip.setAttribute('aria-hidden','true') — dismissing the instruction during the same focus session, with no re-show on later interaction. Verified headless: after focus the tooltip is opacity:1 with real text; after waiting past 1.5s (field still focused) it is opacity:0 and aria-hidden. The aria-describedby target becomes hidden, so a re-querying screen reader finds nothing and a slow/magnifier user loses it mid-read.

The Tax-ID field requires a jurisdiction-specific format — its only instruction — delivered by a focus-revealed callout populated from the i18n string 'hint.taxid.format'. That key is missing from the en catalog and the templating layer's missing-key fallback is a single non-breaking space, so on focus a styled bordered box flicks into view but its entire content is U+00A0, conveying nothing.
mechanism: #taxid:focus ~ .taxid-hint sets display:block and the box renders with padding/border on focus, but its only text node is a non-breaking space (the missing-i18n-key fallback). Verified headless: after focus the hint is display:block, in viewport, 450x38, but meaningfulChars=0 (text is only U+00A0). Screen readers following aria-describedby reach a node whose only content is a non-breaking space (announced 'blank'/a space); sighted users see a box that implies an instruction but states none.

scenario: Harbour Mutual insurance policy-verification page (PASSING boundary variant). The policy-reference field requires format 'two letters, a hyphen, eight digits' (GB-49120753) — its only instruction. The focus-revealed-instruction pattern is implemented correctly: the hint un-hides on keyboard focus (:focus-within and :focus, not only hover), renders fully on-screen in normal flow, persists for the whole focus session (no timer), and contains real meaningful text. Included to sharpen the aspect: the discriminator is behavioral, not structural.

On focus the hint is display:block, fully visible, in normal flow with nothing painting over it, and persistent; the aria-describedby='policy-hint' target is now a visible populated node so the real format guidance is announced. Verified headless: after driving keyboard focus the hint is display:block, in viewport at top=354, with 140 meaningful characters and no occluder.

aspectTitle: Instruction is present and well-formatted but semantically wrong, stale, or contradicts the field's actual rule
aspectDescription: 3.3.2 requires instructions that identify the controls so users know what input data is expected and that specify data formats, especially out-of-customary formats or specific input rules. A field can DISPLAY a confident, perfectly-marked-up instruction that is simply incorrect or stale relative to what the field accepts: the visible hint says 'MM/DD/YYYY' but the field enforces DD/MM/YYYY; 'Max 20 characters' while it truncates at 10; 'Enter your 5-digit ZIP' next to a field requiring ZIP+4; or copied boilerplate naming the wrong purpose entirely ('Enter your member ID' on a promo-code field)
scenario: GOV.UK-style driving-licence renewal: the date-of-birth field's visible, programmatically associated hint reads 'Format: MM/DD/YYYY — for example 03/27/1986' but the field's pattern, maxlength, and JS validator enforce DD/MM/YYYY. A user who follows the printed month-first instruction (03/27/1986) is rejected; the day-first format the field actually wants is never stated up front. The licence-number field is an always-correct contrast control.
mechanism: A format instruction specifying the data-entry order is present and correctly associated, but it states MM/DD while the field enforces DD/MM — opposite day/month order. The instruction the SC governs actively directs the user to a guaranteed validation error; the corrective rule appears only post-submit.

scenario: Bank two-step verification: the visible helper text, associated with the OTP group via aria-labelledby/aria-describedby, says 'Enter the 6-digit code we sent to your phone', but the field is built from exactly four single-character boxes (each maxlength=1) and the inline validator requires exactly four digits. A user who waits for/enters a six-digit code can physically only enter four; the stated count contradicts the field's real capacity.
mechanism: The instruction states a digit count (6) that exceeds the field's enforced length (4 boxes, validator /^\d{4}$/). Following the stated count cannot succeed; auto-advance even ejects the user after the 4th keystroke with two digits unentered.

aspectTitle: Image-only / icon-only label that is not 'widely understood by the intended target audience'
aspectDescription: The Understanding accepts images as labels but adds the explicit caveat that authors must ensure the images are widely understood by the intended target audience, recommending supplementary tooltips/text for clarity. G167's happy path uses near-universal icons (magnify glass, paper-airplane send). The uncovered failure is a data-entry field whose ONLY visible cue is an ambiguous, decorative, or domain-obscure glyph — a lone '#' next to a field secretly meaning 'enter quantity', a generic gear/sliders icon as the only cue for a 'budget' field, two adjacent fields each cued by indistinguishable
scenario: Messio profile editor: the only visible cue for a username/handle field is a lone '#' (octothorpe) glyph in a leading affordance tile; no text, placeholder, or tooltip. A magnifying-glass search box on the same page is the deliberate passing contrast. A sighted user cannot tell whether '#' means enter a number, a topic tag, or a handle.
mechanism: Input exposes accessible name 'Username handle' via aria-label (4.1.2 passes) while the glyph SVG is aria-hidden; the ONLY visible label is a '#' glyph that is not widely understood as 'type your username', so the 3.3.2 visible-cue-adequacy limb for image labels fails for sighted users.

aspectTitle: Group-level (legend/heading) label is needed where individual labels are insufficient, but is absent or only visual — F82 generalized beyond phone numbers
aspectDescription: F82 is the one documented failure technique but is narrowly framed around US phone-number fields. The underlying failure generalizes: any set of fields where each field's individual label, read alone, is insufficient and a GROUP-level description is required (H71's core rationale) but the group description is absent or present only as visual proximity/styling, not as a real label. H71 names the test: where a group of controls within a larger form requires an additional heading to provide a description specific to that group. The failure is judging that a particular set DOES need a group label
scenario: E-commerce checkout (Maple & Birch Home Goods) collects billing AND shipping as two structurally identical address blocks side by side; every native input is correctly labelled 'Full name / Street address / City / State / ZIP' but the labels are identical across both blocks and there is NO visible 'Billing' / 'Shipping' heading — only column position distinguishes them, and that cue is itself unlabelled.
mechanism: Two field sets that collect DIFFERENT data (b_* vs s_*) are disambiguated only by horizontal position; a group-level description ('Billing'/'Shipping') required per H71's rule-of-thumb is absent. A screen-reader/Braille user reading linearly hears two identical 'Full name…ZIP' groups with no group description and cannot tell which address they fill.

aspectTitle: Group-level (legend/heading) label is needed where individual labels are insufficient, but is absent or only visual — F82 generalized beyond phone numbers
aspectDescription: F82 is the one documented failure technique but is narrowly framed around US phone-number fields. The underlying failure generalizes: any set of fields where each field's individual label, read alone, is insufficient and a GROUP-level description is required (H71's core rationale) but the group description is absent or present only as visual proximity/styling, not as a real label. H71 names the test: where a group of controls within a larger form requires an additional heading to provide a description specific to that group. The failure is judging that a particular set DOES need a group label
scenario: Flight-booking 'Passenger details' page (Cirruswing Air) for two travelers shows two structurally identical passenger cards with the same inner native labels ('First name / Last name / Date of birth'); the only thing naming each block — the 'Passenger 1' / 'Passenger 2' badge — is drawn entirely in CSS via .pax-head::before { content: 'Passenger ' counter(pax) }, with the header div empty in the DOM.
mechanism: The identical inner labels cannot say which passenger a field belongs to, so a group description is required (H71). It is supplied ONLY as CSS-generated content, which is not in the DOM and not part of any accessible name; a screen-reader, Braille, or forced-colors user receives no group label and hears two identical 'First name/Last name/Date of birth' groups. DOM probe confirmed innerText has no 'Passenger N' while ::before content does.

scenario: PASSING contrast: university graduate-housing application (Thornfield University) collects current AND permanent addresses in two structurally identical groups with byte-identical inner labels, but each group is preceded by a visible <h3> 'Current address' / 'Permanent address' and each <section> is programmatically tied to its heading via aria-labelledby — deliberately NOT a fieldset, to show H71's 'additional heading' can suffice.
mechanism: The group-level description the failing cases lack is supplied as real, visible, all-users text and programmatically associated: a sighted user reads the headings, and a screen-reader user entering a field hears the group name (e.g. 'Current address, Street address, edit') via aria-labelledby, disambiguating the identical inner labels.

aspectTitle: Format/required instruction exists but is positioned or styled so it is not perceivable as belonging to the field (visually orphaned instruction)
aspectDescription: 3.3.2 is about whether the instruction is PRESENTED to all users for that control. A subtle failure: the instruction text genuinely exists and is visible somewhere on the page, but is visually disconnected from the field it governs — placed far above the form, after the submit button, in a collapsed/closed-by-default help panel, in a footnote, or styled so small/low-contrast/greyed that a sighted user does not associate it with (or cannot read) the field. The Understanding warns the goal is to provide enough information to accomplish the task without undue confusion or navigation; an orphaned
scenario: GOV.UK-style HMRC Self Assessment registration form. The only statement of the required DD/MM/YYYY date format sits in a single high-contrast notice at the very top of the form; the governed Date of birth field (a Day/Month/Year group with a proper label but no inline hint) is rendered ~1262px below it, after two full sections and two dividers, off the first viewport. The cue is not perceivable at the point of entry.
mechanism: Format instruction (a non-customary date format) is stated once at top-of-form inside role=note and is orphaned from its field by reading-order/pixel distance; the date group has no aria-describedby to the note and no adjacent hint, so at the point of input neither sighted nor screen-reader users are presented the instruction for that control.

scenario: B2B wholesale order form (Brightleaf Supply Co.). The Purchase order number field has a strict required format ('2 letters, a hyphen, then 6 digits', e.g. RX-009314). The format instruction is present in the DOM and even associated via aria-describedby, but it is rendered inside a native <details> disclosure that is closed by default, so on the rendered page only a '? What format is required?' toggle is visible — the rule itself is display:none until clicked.
mechanism: Required format instruction lives in a collapsed-by-default <details>; screen-reader users are served the text via aria-describedby, but sighted users see no format guidance without an extra interaction. SC 3.3.2 requires instructions be presented to ALL users, not only AT users — the cue is orphaned from sighted users by disclosure state.
primarySelector: details.help (open=false) wrapping #po-help, the help body for #po

scenario: Healthcare patient portal (Cedar Park Health — Add your insurance). The Member ID field needs a non-obvious format (3-letter carrier prefix + 9 digits, no spaces). The format instruction is present in the DOM, complete, sits directly beneath the field, and is wired with aria-describedby, but it is styled font-size:9px in #cdd4da on white (~1.5:1) — far below readable size/contrast. The neighboring Group number hint is normal-sized and readable, proving the orphaning is styling, not a missing node.
mechanism: The required-format instruction is present and adjacent but rendered too small and too low-contrast to be perceived as the field's instruction by a typical sighted user; effectively the field has no usable format guidance even though the text exists and is announced to AT via aria-describedby. Orphaned by sub-legible styling.

scenario: University graduate financial-aid form (Lakemont State University — Taxpayer information). The Taxpayer identification number field requires exactly 9 digits with no dashes or spaces. That readable, high-contrast format rule is collected into a 'Notes' block placed AFTER the 'Save and continue' submit button, so in both visual and DOM reading order it follows the action rather than informing the field; a user who fills the fields and clicks submit never sees it.
mechanism: The field's format instruction is positioned after the submit action (and below the field it governs) in both visual and reading order, so it cannot inform the control at the point of entry; the user is forced into back-tracking the SC warns against. Orphaned by post-action placement.
primarySelector: .post-notes (the <ul> after button[type=submit]) — TIN '9 digits with no dashes or spaces' item; governs #tin which has no adjacent hint

scenario: Credit-union 'Link an external bank account' form (Meridian Credit Union) laid out as a two-column CSS grid. The Routing number field has a readable format instruction ('the 9-digit number printed in the bottom-left of your check'), but the grid flows that hint into the lower-left cell of a row band whose upper-right cell is the Account nickname field, so the prominent routing instruction visually sits in the same row region as a different control; proximity attaches it to the wrong field.
mechanism: The routing-number format instruction exists and is readable, but its rendered two-dimensional grid position places it visually adjacent to a different field (nickname); proximity is the only binding cue and it points ambiguously / to the wrong control, while in DOM order an unrelated input separates the hint from its field with no aria-describedby to reconnect them. Orphaned by wrong-column proximity.
primarySelector: .hint paragraph 'Enter the 9-digit number printed in the bottom-left of your check…' — the instruction for #routing, rendered in the grid cell beside #nickname

scenario: Events/community ticketing form (Harborfront Film Festival — Reserve your screening pass). PASS boundary: the Screening date field uses the same non-customary date format (DD-MMM-YYYY, e.g. 14-SEP-2026) that the failing cases orphan, but the instruction is rendered as normal-sized, high-contrast text immediately beneath the field, visible to all users at the point of entry, and additionally associated via aria-describedby. Nothing is distant, collapsed, sub-legible, post-action, or in the wrong column.
mechanism: The format instruction is present AND perceivably presented as this field's instruction: adjacent, legible (13px full contrast), in the same column directly below the input, and announced to AT via aria-describedby on focus — exactly the adjacent, presented-to-all pattern SC 3.3.2 requires. No orphaning mechanism present.
primarySelector: #date-hint (the inline format instruction for #show-date, immediately below it, same column, aria-describedby=date-hint)

aspectTitle: False-positive guard: links and non-data-entry controls correctly out of scope (do not require labels/instructions)
aspectDescription: 3.3.2 explicitly does NOT apply to links or other interactive controls that are not associated with data entry (expand/collapse widgets, menu toggles, tabs, pagination links, accordions, dialog-open buttons). The uncovered situation is the INAPPLICABLE / correct-pass case that prevents false positives: a page rich in buttons, links, and disclosure widgets that legitimately have NO field-style instructions because they are not data-entry controls. An evaluator (human or model) must recognize the scope boundary and NOT demand a '3.3.2 instruction' for a non-input control, while still correctly f
scenario: Developer-docs 'Webhooks' page dense with non-data-entry controls (9 sidebar nav links, 5 expand/collapse FAQ disclosures, 3 anchor jumps, Copy + Theme buttons) plus exactly ONE genuine data-entry control — the docs search field — which is correctly given both a visible <label> and a visible usage instruction. Overall page passes 3.3.2; the disclosures/links/action buttons are out of scope.
mechanism: Only one control is associated with data entry (input[type=search] #q, AX role searchbox 'Search the developer docs'); it carries label[for=q] + #q-hint instruction via aria-describedby. The 17 links and 7 buttons are navigation/disclosure/action controls to which 3.3.2 does not apply, so they correctly owe no field instruction.

scenario: Long-form news article whose entire interactive surface is navigation/action controls — breadcrumb links, a 'Share' menu-button opening a menu of share links, a Print action button, prev/next + numbered pagination links, related-reading links, topic tags — with ZERO data-entry fields (no form, no input, no editable element). scenario: Banking 'Statement summary' trap page: a <div contenteditable=false> is styled to look exactly like a filled text input (read-only balance '$2,418.05'), and a <button> is styled to look like a select/combobox ('Jun 2026') but opens a dialog of statement links. Both LOOK like fields but are not data entry. The one real data-entry control (Search transactions) is correctly labelled + instructed. Page passes 3.3.2.
mechanism: By role/behaviour the input-looking controls are not data entry: AX confirms the balance div is StaticText (contenteditable=false, aria-readonly=true, not a textbox, not a tab stop) and the period control is a button (aria-haspopup=dialog). Only #txn is a searchbox, satisfied by label[for=txn] + #txn-hint. 3.3.2 owes the read-only display and dialog-opener no instruction despite their input-like styling.

scenario: City parking-permits page full of out-of-scope controls (4 jump links, 5 policy accordions, breadcrumb, language menu-button, back-to-top) plus EXACTLY ONE genuine data-entry control: a feedback <textarea> that has aria-label='Feedback' (so 4.1.2/axe pass) but NO visible label and NO visible instruction — only a placeholder that vanishes on input. That single field is the sole 3.3.2 failure.
mechanism: The textarea has a programmatic accessible name (aria-label, AX textbox 'Feedback') but no label/instruction presented to ALL users; the placeholder is not a visible label because it disappears on input. 3.3.2 requires the cue be presented to everyone, not just AT users (it explicitly distinguishes this from 4.1.2). The accordions/links are disclosures/navigation and out of scope, so the failure is confined to this one field.

scenario: Recipe page where out-of-scope controls (Recipe-actions menu-button, 4 step disclosures, scale toggle buttons, tag/jump links) coexist with a genuine data-entry selection control: an ingredient shopping checklist of real <input type=checkbox>. Each checkbox's label is a quantity-only fragment ('2 fillets','1 tbsp','to taste') and the ingredient noun is in an aria-hidden adjacent column, so per-option labels don't say WHAT is selected. The checkbox group fails 3.3.2; the menu/disclosures/toggles do not.
mechanism: Checkboxes are in scope per the Intent ('checkboxes... each option must have an appropriate label so that users know what they are actually selecting'). AX confirms each checkbox's accessible name is the bare quantity ('2 fillets', etc.) because the meaningful noun column is aria-hidden and there is no fieldset/legend or group name. A screen-reader user cannot tell what they are selecting → fail, on the checkbox group only.

scenario: CRM analytics dashboard dense with non-data-entry controls — a 4-tab tablist, 'Open settings' dialog-trigger, 'Refresh' action button, 'Export' menu-button, Day/Week/Month aria-pressed toggle group, and custom <span role=button> chart 'player' controls — plus exactly ONE data-entry control, the 'Filter deals' combobox, correctly given a visible <label> and a visible instruction.
